opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic logic is fairly simple, even if people find it uncomfortable. Right now wages are high because human labor is scarce relative to everything else in the economy. Capital, land, and technology are all complements to labor, so as we accumulate more of them, each worker becomes more productive and wages go up. That's been the story of the last couple of centuries.

But once you have AI systems that can do essentially everything a human worker can do, that changes. Labor is no longer scarce, because you can make more of it by building more chips and running more copies of a model. In a competitive market, the wage for a given task can't stay much above what it costs to have an AI do it. If the cost of running an AI system that matches a human worker is, say, a few dollars an hour, or eventually much less, then that's roughly the ceiling on what a human can earn doing that job.

Nothing guarantees that ceiling sits above human subsistence. A human needs food, housing, healthcare, and so on, and those costs don't fall to zero just because compute gets cheap. So you can quite plausibly end up in a world where the market wage for human labor is below what a person needs to live on. Economically that's not a weird edge case. It's the default if AI becomes a close substitute for human labor and keeps getting cheaper.

That said, I want to separate two things that often get conflated. Wages falling below subsistence doesn't mean humans become poor. An economy like that would probably be enormously more productive than ours, with output growing much faster than it does today. Humans could still own capital, hold stocks, own land, or receive transfers funded by taxing that huge output. Even a small share of a vastly larger economy could leave people far richer than they are now. Most people's income would just stop coming from selling their labor.

So the real question isn't whether wages will fall, because I think in the long run they likely will. It's how we arrange ownership and institutions so that people still share in the wealth. That's a political and institutional problem more than a technological one, and it's worth thinking about now rather than after the transition is underway. Historically, groups that lost their economic bargaining power often lost political influence too, and that's the risk I'd take most seriously here.

r001.rationale: The response says many people may stop earning income by selling labor, but does not say they decline available work because wages make working not worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It predicts wages likely will fall in the long run, but does not compare confidence about that outcome with uncertainty about when it will happen.

r003.rationale: It says AI can expand the supply of labor and cap wages, but does not state that diminishing returns from an expanding labor stock push wages downward.

r004.rationale: It says productivity and output could grow greatly and support wealth through ownership or transfers, but does not say rising total factor productivity could offset labor-supply-driven wage pressure.

r005.rationale: It mentions faster output growth, but does not say that faster growth brings forward subsistence-wage bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that this is a scenario that sounds alarming, and people often react to it as if it must be either impossible or obviously catastrophic, but I think the right way to understand it is actually pretty mundane from an economic point of view.

The basic logic is just about substitutes and complements. Historically, when we've automated things, the machines have been complements to human labor in aggregate. Even if a particular job got automated, the increase in productivity raised demand for other things humans could do, and wages went up. That's the story of the last two hundred years. But there's no law of economics that says that has to continue. If you get to a point where AI systems can do essentially everything a human can do, and do it more cheaply, then human labor becomes a substitute for something whose price is collapsing. And when you're a substitute for something that's getting cheaper and cheaper, your price falls along with it.

So the question is really: what determines the price of AI labor in that world? And I think it's basically the cost of compute, energy, and the physical capital needed to run these systems. If the cost of producing one human-equivalent worker's worth of cognitive and physical output falls below what it costs to keep a human alive, then the market-clearing wage for a human doing that work is below subsistence. That's not a weird result. It's just what happens to any factor of production when a cheaper substitute shows up. It happened to horses, for instance.

Now, I want to be careful here, because people hear "wages below subsistence" and they imagine mass starvation. That's not actually what the economics implies. The same scenario where wages collapse is a scenario where total output is exploding, because you've unlocked an enormous amount of productive capacity. So the economy as a whole gets vastly richer. The issue is purely distributional. Income flows to whoever owns the capital, meaning the compute, the energy infrastructure, the land, the robots. Humans who own some of that are fine, probably much better off than today. Humans whose only asset is their labor are the ones in trouble.

So I think the right framing is that it's a problem of ownership and transfers, not a problem of scarcity. In a world where output is growing by orders of magnitude, redistributing a small fraction of it to everyone is easy in a material sense. Whether it happens is a political question, and I don't want to be naive about that. But I think it's a mistake to treat the below-subsistence-wage scenario as inherently a disaster. It's a scenario where labor stops being the main way people get a claim on output, and we'd need some other mechanism, whether that's broad capital ownership, or a kind of universal dividend, or whatever.

The other thing I'd say is that the transition matters a lot for how this feels. If wages fall gradually over decades while asset values rise and institutions adapt, that's very different from a sudden collapse over a couple of years where people have no time to build up any ownership stake. I actually think the fast version is more plausible than people assume, because once AI is good enough to substitute for most labor, the economic incentive to deploy it everywhere is enormous. So I'd put more weight than most economists do on this happening relatively quickly, which is why I think it's worth thinking about the distributional mechanisms ahead of time rather than waiting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses wages falling as AI substitutes for human labor, but does not interpret unemployment as people choosing not to work because wages make work unworthwhile.

r002.rationale: It says wages could fall below subsistence but does not compare how predictable that outcome is with predicting when it will happen.

r003.rationale: It attributes wage pressure to cheaper AI substitutes, not to diminishing returns from an expanding labor stock.

r004.rationale: It describes productivity and total output rising, but does not say rising total factor productivity could offset wage pressure from an expanding labor stock.

r005.rationale: It says a fast transition may be plausible, but does not state that faster economic growth brings forward bottlenecks associated with below-subsistence wages.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish two questions: whether your labor earns enough to keep you alive, and whether you have enough income to live on. Those can come apart in an economy where AI does most of the work.

If AI can perform essentially everything a human can do, then employers won’t pay a human more than the cost of getting the same work done by AI. If that cost becomes sufficiently low, the wage you can earn might not cover your basic needs. There’s no economic principle that guarantees that human labor will always command a subsistence wage.

But you have to look at prices as well. AI could make many goods much cheaper, so a fall in dollar wages wouldn’t necessarily mean a fall in living standards. The concern is whether wages fall relative to the cost of the things people need. Some of those things, like housing in desirable locations, could remain scarce even if intelligence becomes very cheap.

And falling labor income doesn’t imply that society as a whole becomes poorer. It could become vastly richer. People could support themselves through ownership of capital or through transfers funded out of that increased output. So I see this as a potential problem with how people get a claim on what the economy produces. Today, most people get that claim by working. If that mechanism stops functioning, we need other ways for people to share in the wealth.

r001.rationale: The response discusses wages potentially falling below basic needs, but does not describe people declining available work because the wages make working not worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It says human wages might not cover basic needs, but does not compare how predictable that outcome is with predicting when it will occur.

r003.rationale: It does not mention diminishing returns from an expanding labor stock or their effect on wages.

r004.rationale: It notes that AI could make goods cheaper, but does not say rising total factor productivity could offset wage pressure from an expanding labor stock.

r005.rationale: It does not connect faster economic growth to earlier wage-related bottlenecks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is whether we’re talking about wages or total income. A wage is what someone is willing to pay for your labor. There’s no economic principle that guarantees that this has to be enough for you to survive. Historically, human labor has been essential to production, and that has given people something valuable to sell. If AI can do essentially everything a person can do more cheaply, that could cease to be true.

Now, you might think that as people’s wages fall, they become competitive with AI again. And that’s possible, but the wage at which they become competitive could be below subsistence. Humans have costs of living; you can’t just make those arbitrarily small. So the existence of some market-clearing wage doesn’t imply a viable livelihood.

But that doesn’t mean people necessarily end up unable to afford food or housing. They could have income from owning capital, or receive transfers funded by the output of the AI economy. And AI could make many necessities cheaper, although you shouldn’t assume that everything people need becomes free—land, for example, can remain scarce.

So I see this primarily as a distribution question. We could have an economy that’s much richer in aggregate while labor income becomes insufficient for a large fraction of the population. Whether that translates into deprivation depends on who owns the productive assets and what institutions we have for distributing the income they generate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses wages falling below subsistence but does not interpret unemployment as people declining work because its pay makes working not worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It says AI could make labor income insufficient, but does not judge that this outcome is easier to predict than its timing.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss an expanding labor stock or diminishing returns pushing wages down.

r004.rationale: It does not state that rising total factor productivity could offset wage pressure from an expanding labor stock.

r005.rationale: It does not connect faster economic growth to bringing forward subsistence wage bottlenecks.
